word: The LORD Gave, and the LORD Hath Taken Away
pronunciation: thuh LORD GAYV and thuh LORD hath TAY-kun uh-WAY
pos: n. phr. (Job's confession at the loss of all he had)
etymology: Hebrew YHWH nāthan wa'YHWH lāqāch — nāthan, to give, and lāqach, to take, set side by side under one Subject; the AV keeps the bare parallel and adds nothing to soften it.
biblical_def: The words are Job's, spoken standing, with his mantle rent and his head shaven, in the hour the messengers finished their report: oxen and asses driven off, sheep burned, camels taken, and all ten children dead under a fallen house. He does not say that the Sabeans took, or the Chaldeans, or the wind from the wilderness, though each had done its work. He names one Giver and one Taker and they are the same Person. This is not resignation to fate and it is not stoicism; the next clause is blessed be the name of the LORD, which is worship, and the verse after it records that in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly. The confession rests on two things Scripture holds together without embarrassment. The first is that everything Job had was given, never owned absolutely — children, flocks and health alike came out of the open hand of God and were held on His terms. The second is that the hand which gives is the hand which takes, and that it remains righteous in both motions. Job later speaks rashly and is answered out of the whirlwind, but he is never reproved for this. It stands as the church's pattern for bereavement: not the denial of grief, for Job rent his mantle, but grief that bends the knee.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Give, to bestow; to confer without compensation. Take, to receive what is offered, or to seize, to lay hold on. Job 1:21, the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away.
webster_full: Give, to bestow; to confer without price or compensation.
Take, to lay hold on; to receive back what was lent or lodged.
Hebrew nāthan, to give, bestow, deliver up.
Hebrew lāqach, to take, fetch, lay hold of.
Bless, to praise; to glorify for benefits received. Job 1:21.
scriptures: Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
Job 1:22
In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.
Job 2:10
But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
Jam 5:11
Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.
corruption_summary: The saying is quoted as a shrug at impersonal fate, and the doctrine behind it — that God Himself ordains the taking — is traded for a God who merely permits and is as surprised as the mourner.
corruption_paragraphs: The common modern use empties the line of its Subject. It is offered at funerals as a way of saying that life gives and life takes, that these things happen, that the universe turns. Job says the opposite. He names the LORD twice and makes Him the agent of both verbs, and it is precisely because a Person and not a process stands behind the loss that the sentence can end in blessing. One cannot bless a process. The comfort in the verse is not that loss is natural but that it is governed, and governed by One whose name Job already knows.

The second corruption is more respectable and more damaging. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) and the wider evangelical instinct that God only permits what He does not will would have us say that God did not take Job's children, that Satan did, and that God was grieved alongside Job as a fellow sufferer. The narrative forbids it. Satan acts only within a boundary God sets and twice extends, and the inspired verdict on Job's confession is that he sinned not, nor charged God foolishly — which would be a strange verdict if he had just attributed to God a work God did not do. A God who merely permits cannot be blessed for the taking, and the mourner who is told so is left with grief and no one to worship in it.
roots_summary: Hebrew nāthan, to give, and lāqach, to take — one Subject governs both verbs, and the clause that follows is blessing, not complaint.
roots_lines: Hebrew nāthan, to give, bestow, set, deliver.
Hebrew lāqach, to take, seize, fetch, receive.
The verbs share one Subject: the covenant name, YHWH.
Naked came I out of my mother's womb is the premise — nothing was owned, all was lent.
Blessed be the name of the LORD is the conclusion; the verse ends in worship, Job 1:21.
usage: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD
in all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly
shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?

pos: n. phr. (the counsel of Job's wife on the ash heap)
etymology: Hebrew bārak 'elōhīm wāmūth — the verb is bārak, to bless, used here in the bitter sense of taking leave of God, as a servant blesses his master in parting; the AV renders the sense rather than the bare word.
biblical_def: Job sits among the ashes, smitten with sore boils from the sole of his foot to his crown, scraping himself with a potsherd, and his wife puts to him the shortest argument against God in Scripture: Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die. It is not atheism. She does not doubt that God is there or that He has done this; she grants both and concludes that such a God is not worth keeping faith with. The counsel is therefore the exact thing Satan had predicted twice in the heavenly court — he will curse thee to thy face — now spoken not by the adversary but out of Job's own house and by the one person left to him. Job's answer does not condemn her as the wicked but as one of the foolish, and it refuses the premise rather than the grief: What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? The logic is covenantal. A man who took prosperity as a gift cannot take adversity as an injustice, because he never held the first by right. The temptation she voices is the one every sufferer meets: to make the goodness of God conditional on the comfort of the believer, and, finding the comfort gone, to let the goodness go with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Curse, to utter a wish of evil against; to blaspheme. Die, to cease to live. Job 2:9, the counsel of Job's wife, and the temptation Satan had foretold.
webster_full: Curse, to utter a wish of evil against one; to imprecate evil upon.
Curse, to blaspheme; to treat with contempt that which is holy.
Die, to cease to live; to expire; to lose life.
Hebrew bārak, to bless, and by a bitter euphemism, to take leave of.
Integrity, uprightness; entireness of moral principle. Job 2:9.
scriptures: Job 2:9
Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.
Job 2:10
But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
Job 1:11
But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face.
Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
corruption_summary: The verse is read as proof that Scripture permits a faith that curses, or Job's wife is rehabilitated into an honest voice of protest whose counsel the text is supposed to respect.
corruption_paragraphs: A line of modern exposition treats Job's wife as the book's truth-teller: the one who refuses pious evasion and says what the sufferer really feels, with Job's reply read as repression. The text gives no such reading. Job calls her speech the speech of the foolish — the biblical fool, the one who has said in his heart there is no God worth fearing — and the narrator immediately adds that in all this did not Job sin with his lips. Scripture is not squeamish about lament; the Psalter is full of it, and Job himself will shortly curse the day of his birth. But lament addresses God and holds on; this counsel lets go. The difference is the whole book.

The second misuse runs the other way and makes the verse a club. Because the counsel was wicked, grief itself is treated as suspect, and sufferers in the church are hurried past their losses with a demand for cheerfulness. Job rent his mantle, shaved his head, sat seven days in silence and spoke at last in bitterness of soul, and God's verdict at the end was that Job had spoken of Him the thing that was right. The sin his wife urged was not sorrow but apostasy. The entry to recover is that a believer may sit in ashes and say hard things to God, and that the one road he may not take is the road out.
roots_summary: Hebrew bārak, to bless — used euphemistically for taking leave of God; the counsel is apostasy, not lament, and Job answers it from covenant, not from stoicism.
roots_lines: Hebrew bārak, to bless, kneel, salute; here by euphemism, to renounce.
Hebrew mūth, to die; the counsel joins renunciation to death as one act.
Hebrew tūmmāh, integrity, completeness — what she urges him to drop.
Satan had twice foretold this exact word, Job 1:11 and Job 2:5.
Job answers from the covenant: we received good, we shall receive evil, Job 2:10.
usage: Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die
thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh
in all this did not Job sin with his lips

pos: n. phr. (the angelic chorus at the founding of the earth, Job 38:7)
etymology: Hebrew kōkbē bōqer — stars of the morning; set in parallel with b'nē 'elōhīm, the sons of God, so that the stars of the first line and the angels of the second name one company.
biblical_def: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind by taking him back before there was a Job to ask questions: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? The measuring line is stretched, the corner stone is fastened, and at that moment, the text says, the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy. Hebrew parallelism identifies the two halves: the morning stars are the sons of God, the angelic host, named by the brightest thing in a dark sky because that is what they were at the dawn of the world. The point of the question is not astronomy but witness. Creation had spectators and Job was not among them; the only creatures who saw the foundation laid responded not with analysis but with music. Two things follow for the book's argument. First, the world is older than the sufferer and was not built to his specification, so his demand for an accounting assumes a standing he does not have. Second, the creation was greeted with joy by those who did see it, which quietly answers the charge that the world is badly made. The passage is also the clearest scriptural warrant that the angels were created before the material heavens and earth were finished, and that worship, not silence, was heaven's first response to the works of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Morning, the first part of the day, beginning at twelve o'clock at night. Star, an apparently luminous body in the heavens. Job 38:7, the angelic host at the founding of the earth.
webster_full: Morning, the first part of the day; the dawn; the beginning.
Star, a luminous body appearing in the heavens; figuratively, an illustrious person.
Sing, to utter sounds with melodious modulations of voice.
Hebrew kōkab, a star; bōqer, morning, daybreak.
Sons of God, in Job the angelic host that attends the throne. Job 1:6; Job 38:7.
scriptures: Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
Job 38:6
Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof;
Job 38:7
When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
Praise ye him, all his angels: praise ye him, all his hosts.
corruption_summary: The line is detached from its question and made a piece of cosmic poetry about the music of the spheres, or the sons of God are read as rival deities surviving from a polytheistic source.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as free-standing verse, the morning stars become a metaphor for the harmony of nature and the passage is used to baptise whatever a given age believes about the cosmos — Pythagorean spheres once, an impersonal evolving universe now. The verse will not detach. It is the second line of an interrogation, and its force depends entirely on the first: Where wast thou? The singing is evidence in a case against Job's competence to judge God, and the comfort it finally gives him is not aesthetic but personal.

The historical-critical handling takes sons of God as a fossil of Canaanite polytheism, a divine council of lesser gods imperfectly scrubbed by later editors. The book itself gives the phrase its meaning without help: in Job 1:6 and 2:1 the sons of God present themselves before the LORD as servants before a throne, and Satan comes among them as one accountable. They are creatures attending their Maker, not colleagues. Scripture elsewhere commands the same host to praise Him — praise ye him, all his angels — which is the opposite of a pantheon. The principle to recover is that Job 38 is one God speaking, and the stars that sang were made the same week as the ground Job sat on.
roots_summary: Hebrew kōkbē bōqer, stars of the morning, set in parallel with the sons of God — one angelic company, singing at the laying of the foundations.
roots_lines: Hebrew kōkab, a star; bōqer, morning or dawn.
Hebrew b'nē 'elōhīm, sons of God — in Job, the angelic host.
Hebrew rānan, to give a ringing cry; here rendered sang together.
Hebrew rūa', to shout, raise a war cry or a shout of joy.
The corner stone of Job 38:6 is laid before any man exists to see it.
usage: the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy
where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?
whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened?

word: My Spirit Shall Not Always Strive With Man
pronunciation: my SPIR-it shal not AWL-wayz STRYV with MAN
pos: n. phr. (the LORD's word before the flood, Genesis 6:3)
etymology: Hebrew lō'-yādōn rūachī bā'ādām l''ōlām — the verb dīn carries the sense of pleading a case or contending in judgment, hence the AV's strive.
biblical_def: The sentence is spoken as the earth fills with violence and the imagination of man's heart is only evil continually: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years. Two things are declared. The first is that the Spirit's striving has a term. God had not been silent before the flood — Enoch walked with Him and prophesied, Noah is called a preacher of righteousness, and the Spirit pressed the case against that generation through its conscience and its preachers. The second is that the term is now set: a hundred and twenty years, the span of Noah's building and preaching, after which the door would shut. The verse is therefore the Bible's plainest statement that the patience of God is real, is long, and is not endless. Peter makes the same point twice, once to say that the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah while the ark was preparing, and once to say that the Lord is not slack concerning His promise but longsuffering to usward. The striving of the Spirit with a man or a generation is mercy, not threat; the warning lies in the word always, and in the fact that when the hundred and twenty years ran out it was the LORD who shut the door.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Strive, to contend; to struggle in opposition. Always, perpetually; continually. Genesis 6:3, the limit set to the Spirit's contending with the antediluvian world.
webster_full: Strive, to make efforts; to contend; to struggle in opposition.
Always, perpetually; throughout all time; continually.
Flesh, in Scripture, man's corrupt and sinful nature.
Hebrew dīn, to judge, plead a cause, contend in judgment.
Longsuffering, bearing injuries long without anger. 1 Peter 3:20.
scriptures: Gen 6:3
And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.
Gen 6:5
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
Act 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
corruption_summary: The verse is read as a statement about the human lifespan only, emptying it of warning; or God's patience is made infinite in principle, so that the door of the ark never truly shuts.
corruption_paragraphs: A common reading takes the hundred and twenty years as a new cap on human longevity and stops there. The chapter does not support it: men after the flood live well past that figure, and the context is a verdict on a generation, not a change to human biology. The number is the length of a reprieve. Noah is told to build, and the building is itself the sermon. To read the verse as demography is to delete the only reason it was spoken, which was to date the end of mercy for people who still had time to repent.

The graver corruption is the drift toward a God whose patience has no term. Universalism in its older form, and the softer modern assumption that there will always be another chance, both require that the Spirit strive always. Scripture says He will not. Stephen charges the council with resisting the Holy Ghost as their fathers did, and the flood stands behind that charge as the proof that resistance can succeed in the only sense that matters: the resister is finally let alone. The doctrine to recover is that the longsuffering of God is a season and not a standing condition, and that the ark had a door which was shut from the outside.
roots_summary: Hebrew dīn, to contend or plead in judgment — the Spirit pleads with men for a term, and the hundred and twenty years is that term.
roots_lines: Hebrew rūach, spirit, breath, wind; here the Spirit of God.
Hebrew dīn, to judge or plead a cause; the AV renders it strive.
Hebrew l''ōlām, for ever or always — the word the sentence denies.
Flesh here is moral, not merely bodily: man also is flesh.
The hundred and twenty years are the span of Noah's preaching, 1 Peter 3:20.
usage: my spirit shall not always strive with man
yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years
the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah

word: Ye Thought Evil Against Me, But God Meant It Unto Good
pronunciation: YEE THAWT EE-vul uh-GENST mee but GOD MENT it UN-too GUUD
pos: n. phr. (Joseph's word to his brethren, Genesis 50:20)
etymology: Hebrew 'attem chashabtem 'ālay rā'āh 'elōhīm chashābāh l'tōbāh — one verb, chāshab, to devise or purpose, is used of both parties; the AV varies the English, rendering it first ‘thought’ and then ‘meant’, but the Hebrew makes the parallel exact.
biblical_def: Jacob is buried and the brothers, afraid that Joseph has only been waiting for their father to die, send a message and then fall before his face offering themselves as servants. Joseph weeps and answers, Fear not: for am I in the place of God? — and then names what they did and what God did: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. The Hebrew uses one verb for both clauses, so that the brothers' devising and God's devising are set in deliberate parallel over a single set of events. This is the Bible's plainest statement of concurrence: the same act is genuinely the brothers' crime and genuinely God's work, without the crime ceasing to be crime or the work ceasing to be good. Joseph does not say that God made the best of a bad business, nor that the evil was secretly good. He says they meant it for evil and are guilty of it, and that God meant the identical event for good and accomplished it. The pattern is repeated at Calvary, where Peter tells Jerusalem that Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that they took Him and by wicked hands crucified and slew Him. Both halves are required, and neither is permitted to swallow the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Mean, to intend; to purpose; to design. Evil, that which produces pain, calamity, or moral wrong. Genesis 50:20, the brothers' design and God's design over one event.
webster_full: Mean, to have in the mind; to intend; to purpose; to design.
Evil, having bad qualities of a moral kind; wicked; corrupt.
Good, that which contributes to the benefit and happiness of men.
Hebrew chāshab, to think, devise, reckon, purpose — used of both parties.
Save alive, to preserve from death. Genesis 50:20.
scriptures: And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
Gen 45:5
Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.
Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
corruption_summary: The verse is flattened into the maxim that everything happens for a reason, which excuses the brothers; or God's hand is reduced to reaction, so that He redeems a situation He did not ordain.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimental use of this verse is the modern proverb that all things work out in the end, which comforts no one who has been genuinely wronged because it quietly tells them that the wrong was not so bad. Joseph says the opposite. Ye thought evil is an indictment, delivered to the men's faces, and they are on the ground in front of him when he says it. The verse does not dissolve guilt into providence; it holds the two together and lets the guilty go free on the ground of mercy, not on the ground that nothing really happened.

The opposite corruption is now the more common in evangelical teaching: God did not intend Joseph's pit or his prison, but He is very good at redeeming what others ruin. The grammar forbids it. The same verb governs both clauses, and Joseph had already told his brothers in Genesis 45 that it was not they that sent him thither but God. Open theism must deny this verse outright; the broader instinct that will not let God ordain what men do wickedly must at least silence it. The doctrine to recover is concurrence — that God ordains the end and the means without becoming the author of sin, and that the clearest proof is a cross which was at once the determinate counsel of God and the worst act in human history.
roots_summary: Hebrew chāshab, to devise or purpose, governs both clauses — one event, two intentions, the brothers guilty and God good.
roots_lines: Hebrew chāshab, to think, plan, devise, impute.
The verb is identical in both halves; the AV varies the English only.
Hebrew rā'āh, evil or calamity; tōbāh, good.
Am I in the place of God? — Joseph refuses the office of avenger, Genesis 50:19.
The same double intention appears at the cross, Acts 2:23.
usage: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good
to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive
it was not you that sent me hither, but God

word: The LORD Shall Fight for You, and Ye Shall Hold Your Peace
pronunciation: thuh LORD shal FYT for YOO and YEE shal HOHLD yor PEES
pos: n. phr. (Moses to Israel at the Red Sea, Exodus 14:14)
etymology: Hebrew YHWH yillāchēm lākem w''attem tacharishūn — lācham, to fight or do battle, and chārash, to be silent or hold still; the AV's hold your peace renders a command to silence, not merely to calm.
biblical_def: Israel is pinned between Pihahiroth and the sea with the chariots of Egypt closing, and the people turn on Moses with the bitter complaint that there were graves enough in Egypt without being brought to the wilderness to die. Moses answers: Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day — and then, The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace. Three imperatives govern the sentence: fear not, stand still, be silent. The nation is not told to arm or to negotiate but to stop talking and watch. This is not quietism, for God immediately tells Moses to speak to the children of Israel that they go forward, and Moses must stretch out his hand over the sea; obedience is required and the sea is crossed on foot. What is forbidden is the murmuring, and what is promised is that the battle belongs to the LORD. The pattern recurs: Moses reminds the next generation that the LORD their God went before them and fought for them in Egypt; Jahaziel tells Jehoshaphat's army that the battle is not theirs but God's and that they shall not need to fight but stand still and see. The sentence has rightly become the church's word for every extremity in which no human action remains.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Fight, to contend in battle; to make war. Hold one's peace, to be silent; to forbear to speak. Exodus 14:14, the word to Israel at the sea.
webster_full: Fight, to strive or contend for victory in battle or in single combat.
Hold one's peace, to be silent; to forbear speaking.
Stand still, to remain fixed; to stop; to cease from motion.
Hebrew lācham, to fight, do battle, engage in war.
Hebrew chārash, to be silent, be still, keep quiet. Exodus 14:14.
scriptures: And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever.
The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
Deu 1:30
The LORD your God which goeth before you, he shall fight for you, according to all that he did for you in Egypt before your eyes;

Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you, O Judah and Jerusalem: fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you.
corruption_summary: The verse is made a charter for passivity in every circumstance, or it is reduced to a slogan of self-assurance that the believer's plans will prosper.
corruption_paragraphs: Quoted alone, the line has been used to justify doing nothing in the face of duty — declining to work, to provide, to resist evil, or to take ordinary lawful means, on the ground that one is waiting on God. The chapter refuses it. Within two verses the LORD asks Moses why he cries unto Him and commands the people to go forward, and the sea opens only as Moses stretches out his hand. The silence commanded was the end of murmuring against Moses, not the end of obedience. Scripture elsewhere sets men in array and expects them to fight; what it never permits is the fear that argues with God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the limit of the promise. The LORD fought for Israel at the sea because He had covenanted to bring that nation out, and the modern habit of lifting the line onto any venture a believer has undertaken — a business, a lawsuit, a campaign — borrows a guarantee that was never given. The believer's warrant for quietness is not that his plans will succeed but that his God is righteous and that he is commanded to stand still in the place God has actually put him.
roots_summary: Hebrew lācham, to fight, with chārash, to be silent — the LORD takes the battle and Israel is commanded to stop murmuring, not to stop obeying.
roots_lines: Hebrew lācham, to fight or wage war; the Subject is YHWH.
Hebrew chārash, to be silent, still, speechless.
Hebrew y'shū'āh, salvation or deliverance — the salvation of the LORD.
Stand still is a command against murmuring, not against obedience: compare Exodus 14:15.
Jahaziel repeats the pattern before Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 20:17.
usage: the LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace
stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD
the LORD your God which goeth before you, he shall fight for you

word: Thou Shalt Not Seethe a Kid in His Mother's Milk
pronunciation: thow SHALT not SEETH uh KID in hiz MUTH-urz MILK
etymology: Hebrew lō'-t'bashshēl g'dī bachalēb 'immō — bāshal, to boil or seethe; g'dī, a kid of the goats; the precept stands three times, twice attached to the feast of firstfruits and once to the law of clean food.
biblical_def: The precept appears three times in the Law and always in the same company. Twice it closes the command to bring the first of the firstfruits into the house of the LORD, and once it closes the law distinguishing what Israel may eat. No reason is given in the text, which is itself part of the point: Israel is to obey because the LORD has spoken, and a people who will keep only the commands they can explain have not yet learned what obedience is. What can be said from Scripture is this. The kid and its mother's milk belong to one order of nature; the milk was given to nourish the young, and to use it to boil the young is to turn a creature's own provision into the instrument of its seething. The Law repeatedly guards such boundaries — the ox and the ass are not yoked together, the field is not sown with mingled seed, the dam is not taken with her young from the nest. Israel's God is not careless about the orders He made, and His people were to be marked by a tenderness toward creation that the nations around them did not share. Placed beside the firstfruits, the precept says that the worship of the LORD is not to be mixed with cruelty, nor His gifts turned against the creatures that bore them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Seethe, to boil; to decoct in hot liquor. Kid, a young goat. Exodus 23:19, the precept thrice repeated in the Law.
webster_full: Seethe, to boil; to decoct or prepare for food in hot liquor.
Kid, a young goat; the young of the goat kind.
Firstfruits, the first produce of the earth offered to God.
Hebrew bāshal, to boil, seethe, ripen, bring to maturity.
Hebrew g'dī, a kid; chālāb, milk. Exodus 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21.
scriptures: The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring unto the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.

Ye shall not eat of any thing that dieth of itself: thou shalt give it unto the stranger that is in thy gates, that he may eat it; or thou mayest sell it unto an alien: for thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
Deu 22:6

If a bird's nest chance to be before thee in the way in any tree, or on the ground, whether they be young ones, or eggs, and the dam sitting upon the young, or upon the eggs, thou shalt not take the dam with the young:
corruption_summary: The precept is explained away as a mere polemic against a Canaanite rite and so emptied of binding force, or it is inflated into the whole rabbinic separation of meat and milk.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern explanation is that the line forbids a specific Canaanite or Ugaritic fertility rite, and that once the rite is identified the precept has been accounted for and may be set aside. Two things are wrong with it. The first is evidential: no such rite has been established from the texts appealed to, and the explanation has been repeated far more confidently than the sources permit. The second is theological: even if a pagan practice stood behind it, a law given by God to His people is not disposed of by naming what it opposed. Scripture itself gives no reason here, and the honest reader leaves it where the text leaves it — as a command, set beside the firstfruits, from a God who has the right to be obeyed without explaining Himself.

The opposite error builds a vast structure on the sentence. Rabbinic tradition extended it into the full separation of meat and milk, with separate vessels and waiting periods, and treated the extension as binding. This is the very practice our Lord named when He charged the Pharisees with making the commandment of God of none effect by their tradition. The precept says what it says, three times, about a kid and its mother's milk. The principle to recover is that a plain command is neither to be dissolved by a clever origin story nor enlarged into a fence that becomes heavier than the law it was built to guard.
roots_summary: Hebrew bāshal, to seethe or boil, with g'dī, a kid, and chālāb, milk — a boundary of nature guarded, and set beside the firstfruits.

word: As a Man Chasteneth His Son
pronunciation: az uh MAN CHAY-sun-eth hiz SUN
pos: n. phr. (the lesson of the wilderness, Deuteronomy 8:5)
etymology: Hebrew ka'asher y'yassser 'īsh 'eth-b'nō — yāsar, to discipline, instruct or correct, from which mūsār, instruction or chastening, is formed; the word joins teaching and correction in one idea.
biblical_def: Moses is explaining the forty years to a generation about to enter the land: the LORD led them, humbled them, suffered them to hunger and fed them with manna, and their raiment waxed not old upon them. Then the conclusion: Thou shalt also consider in thine heart, that, as a man chasteneth his son, so the LORD thy God chasteneth thee. The figure settles the question of motive. The hardship of the wilderness was not the anger of a creditor nor the indifference of fate, but the hand of a Father on a son He intends to bring somewhere. Hebrew yāsar covers both instruction and correction, which is why the manna is part of the chastening as much as the hunger was: the point of both was to teach that man doth not live by bread only but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD. Two guards belong to the doctrine. It applies to sons, not to the world at large; chastening is a mark of standing in the family, and Hebrews draws exactly that line — if ye be without chastisement, then are ye bastards, and not sons. And it is not proof of a particular sin, for the generation was humbled to be proved and to be taught, not merely punished. Solomon states the ground: whom the LORD loveth he correcteth, even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Chasten, to correct by punishment; to afflict for the purpose of reclaiming. Deuteronomy 8:5, the wilderness read as a father's discipline.
webster_full: Chasten, to correct by punishment; to punish for the purpose of reclaiming.
Chasten, to afflict by other means; to purify from errors or faults.
Humble, to abase; to bring low; to reduce the pride of.
Hebrew yāsar, to discipline, instruct, correct, admonish.
Hebrew mūsār, instruction or chastening. Proverbs 3:11-12.
scriptures: Deu 8:3

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
Deu 8:5
Thou shalt also consider in thine heart, that, as a man chasteneth his son, so the LORD thy God chasteneth thee.
Pro 3:12
For whom the LORD loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.
Heb 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: Chastening is recast as divine abuse and rejected outright, or it is turned into a rule that every affliction is punishment for a traceable sin.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic reading now treats the whole doctrine as damaging: a God who chastens is read as a punitive parent, and the texts are either set aside or reinterpreted so that God merely allows consequences. Scripture will not be handled that way. Hebrews takes the father-and-son figure and presses it harder, not softer, and makes chastening the evidence of sonship rather than the embarrassment of it — whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. The alternative on offer is not a kinder God but an indifferent one, which is the condition Hebrews calls bastardy. A father who will not correct has not spared his son anything; he has only declined to own him. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: the entry names the therapeutic objection in order to answer it

The opposite error is the friends' error in Job, and it is alive in the churches: every affliction is read as the penalty of some particular sin, and the sufferer is set to hunting for the cause. Deuteronomy 8 gives the wilderness a different purpose — to humble, to prove, to teach dependence, and to do the nation good at the latter end. Our Lord refused the same inference twice, over the man born blind and over the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled. The principle to recover is that chastening is fatherly, purposeful and proportioned, that it belongs to sons, and that its aim is stated plainly: that we might be partakers of His holiness.

pos: n. phr. (of Israel's going out of Egypt, and of presumptuous sin)
etymology: Hebrew b'yād rāmāh — with a lifted or raised hand; rūm, to be high or exalted. The same phrase carries two opposite senses in the Law, according to whose hand is lifted.
biblical_def: The AV keeps one idiom for two very different things, and the difference is everything. In Exodus and Numbers it describes the manner of the exodus: the children of Israel went out with an high hand — openly, in the sight of all the Egyptians, not slipping away by night as fugitives but marching out as a people redeemed, with the hand of their God lifted over them. It is a phrase of triumph and of public vindication, and it belongs to the LORD before it belongs to Israel; the psalmist praises Him who brought out Israel with a strong hand and a stretched out arm. In Numbers 15 the same words name the worst class of sin. Having provided offerings for the soul that sinneth through ignorance, the Law turns: the soul that doeth ought presumptuously — Hebrew, with an high hand — the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people. There the lifted hand is the sinner's own, raised in defiance against God, and for it the sacrificial system makes no provision. The idiom thus marks the two directions a raised hand can take: God's hand lifted for His people in redemption, and a man's hand lifted against God in presumption.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): High-handed, overbearing; oppressive; violent. Hand, in Scripture, power, might, and the instrument of action. Exodus 14:8; Numbers 15:30.
webster_full: High, elevated; lifted up; raised above a surface or the common level.
High-handed, overbearing; oppressive; violent; arbitrary.
Hand, in Scripture, power, might, the instrument by which a work is done.
Hebrew rūm, to be high, rise, be lifted up or exalted.
Presumptuously, with bold and insolent confidence. Numbers 15:30.
scriptures: Exo 14:8
And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued after the children of Israel: and the children of Israel went out with an high hand.
Num 33:3

And they departed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the morrow after the passover the children of Israel went out with an high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians.
But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people.
With a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm: for his mercy endureth for ever.
corruption_summary: The idiom is levelled into a single sense, so that the triumph of the exodus and the defiance of presumptuous sin are no longer distinguished; and presumptuous sin itself is softened into mere mistake.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern versions frequently render the two occurrences with unrelated English, which is defensible translation but costs the reader the deliberate echo. In Hebrew the same hand is raised in both places, and the Law intends the comparison: a people brought out under God's lifted hand are the last people who may lift their own against Him. Where the echo is lost, Numbers 15 reads as an isolated severity instead of the natural answer to Exodus 14, and the reader misses that presumption is not merely disobedience but the reversal of redemption's own gesture.

The more serious corruption is the quiet disappearance of the category. Numbers 15 distinguishes sin through ignorance, for which an offering is appointed, from sin with an high hand, for which none is, and the New Testament keeps the distinction in its own terms when it speaks of sinning wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth. A pastoral culture that treats all sin as weakness, inherited damage or poor choices has no way to name defiance, and therefore no way to call a man out of it. Scripture is tender toward the ignorant and the straying and hard toward the presumptuous, and the two must not be levelled. The principle to recover is that there is a sin which reproaches the LORD, and that the warning is mercy to the man still able to hear it.
roots_summary: Hebrew b'yād rāmāh, with a lifted hand — of Israel marching out in triumph, and of the sinner raising his hand against God.
